title: Tofu vs. tempeh: protein and nutrition differences

seo.title: Tofu vs. tempeh: protein and nutrition differences
seo.meta_description: Tempeh is usually higher in protein and fiber because it retains the whole soybean and contains less water. Tofu may provide much more calcium.
seo.search_intent: Compare tofu and tempeh for protein, calories, fiber, fat, fermentation, calcium, and practical use.

excerpt: Tempeh is usually more protein-dense than tofu, at roughly 19–20 grams per 100 grams versus about 12–17 grams in firm tofu. Much of the difference comes from retaining the whole soybean and containing less water. Tempeh also provides more fiber, while tofu is usually lower in calories and can contain far more calcium when set with calcium salts.
content_html:
Tofu and tempeh start with the same legume but look and behave very differently by the time they reach the plate. Tofu is made from coagulated soy milk; tempeh ferments mostly intact soybeans. That processing difference explains much of what later shows up on the nutrition label.

Tempeh is usually more concentrated in protein and fiber; tofu contains more water, is generally lower in calories and can provide much more calcium depending on how it was set.

Tempeh is more concentrated per 100 grams

Per 100 gFirm tofuPlain tempeh
Protein~12–17 g~19–20 g
Calories~120–145~190–200
Fat~7–9 g~10–11 g
Fiber~1–3 g~4–7 g

The protein difference is real, but it does not appear because fermentation “creates” a large amount of new protein. Tempeh retains the whole soybean and contains less water by weight, so nutrients are more concentrated.

Serving size can bring total protein surprisingly close

About 5 ounces of tempeh at 19.5 grams of protein per 100 grams provides roughly 28 grams of protein. Around 7 ounces of tofu at 15 grams per 100 grams provides about 30 grams.

That is the useful way to read the table: tempeh is denser, but a somewhat larger serving of tofu can deliver a very similar amount of protein.

Fiber tells an important part of the story

Making tofu filters out much of the soybean pulp, taking a substantial amount of insoluble fiber with it. In tempeh, most of the bean remains in the finished food.

That is why tempeh commonly provides several more grams of fiber per 100 grams and also has a much firmer, chewier texture. Tofu can range from silken to extra-firm and behaves very differently in cooking.

Fermented does not automatically mean probiotic

Tempeh is fermented with molds in the Rhizopus genus. Fermentation changes proteins and carbohydrates and can reduce some antinutritional compounds.

But tempeh is normally cooked before eating. Heat reduces or kills many live microorganisms, so cooked tempeh should not automatically be described as a source of live probiotics.

Calcium can flip the comparison

Tofu set with calcium sulfate can provide several hundred milligrams of calcium per 100 grams. Tempeh generally contains much less.

The catch is that not every tofu uses the same coagulant. Two blocks that look identical can have very different calcium content, which makes the label genuinely useful here.

Both provide complete protein

Both tofu and tempeh come from soy and contain all nine essential amino acids. Neither needs to be combined with rice or another grain at the same meal to “complete” its protein.

Tempeh also should not be treated as a dependable vitamin B12 source. B12 content can be variable and does not replace fortified foods or supplements when a reliable source is needed.

Which should you choose?

Tempeh makes sense when you want more protein and fiber in a smaller amount of food and like a firm texture. Tofu works well when you prefer a more adaptable texture, lower energy density and, depending on the product, a lot of calcium.

There is no universal winner: tempeh concentrates; tofu gives you more volume and can excel in calcium. Both are excellent plant-protein staples, but they are not nutritionally identical.

faq.question: Which has more protein, tofu or tempeh?
faq.answer: Tempeh usually provides about 19–20 g protein per 100 g versus roughly 12–17 g in firm tofu.

faq.question: Does tempeh have more fiber?
faq.answer: Yes, usually substantially more, because it retains the whole soybean while tofu loses much of the fiber during filtering.

faq.question: Is tempeh probiotic?
faq.answer: It is fermented, but it is normally cooked before eating. Heat reduces live microbes, so cooked tempeh should not be assumed to provide live probiotics.
